summary:
For the people of Guam, in the words of the park’s brochure, war came early and stayed late. Hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor — December 8, 1941, on Guam’s side of the date line — Japan bombed the U.S. territory, and on December 10 Japanese forces invaded. Under the naval police who ruled the island they renamed Omiyajima, English was forbidden, and Chamorros suspected of hiding family members wanted by the Japanese, or of aiding Americans, were harassed, beaten, tortured or executed. In 1944 men, women and children were made to work at bayonet point digging shelter caves and building defenses, and in early July 10,000 to 15,000 Chamorros were marched to jungle camps with little food or water; many did not survive. On July 21, 1944, 55,000 U.S. troops landed on the Asan and Agat beaches, and the island was declared secure on August 10, at a cost, by the brochure’s count, of over 7,000 American and about 17,500 Japanese casualties. [n]

Congress established War in the Pacific National Historical Park on August 18, 1978. Its seven units, around the villages of Asan, Piti and Agat, keep the invasion beaches, pillboxes, caves and gun emplacements — three Japanese coastal guns at Piti were hauled into place by Chamorros under forced labor — along with the remains of refugee camps where thousands of Chamorros were left homeless. A memorial wall above Asan Bay lists the Americans who died defending and retaking Guam and the people of Guam who suffered and died during 31 months of occupation. More than half the park is coral reef, and the Park Service counts it the most biologically diverse unit in the national park system. [n] [n]

indigenous.html:
The Chamorro people, believed to have come from Southeast Asia, set the houses of the affluent atop stone pillars called latte and were, the 2004 administrative history notes, the only people in Oceania known to have grown rice. Under Spanish rule, in September 1671, some 2,000 Chamorros besieged a fortified church for about forty days, and disease and fighting had left about 3,700 people by 1710, the history reports. [n]

After 1898, the history says, the United States turned more than a third of Guam into a military installation under a Navy governor, starting almost seventy years of military control; by Guam government figures, private landholdings fell by more than a quarter from 1950 to 1952 as military holdings grew. In 1977 Congress let the District Court of Guam hear claims over land taken between 1944 and 1963 without fair condemnation. The history concludes that this military control bred deep local resentment and mistrust, the setting in which the park was born. [n]

climate.html: The reef fish that were part of the traditional Chamorro diet are still taken for food today, and the reefs are warming. Guam’s shallow reefs bleached every year from 2013 to 2017; heat stress and extreme low tides during the 2014–2015 El Niño ravaged branching Acropora corals on the island’s reef flats, including a site in the park’s Asan unit, and 2017 was the worst year on record for heat stress and bleaching. The Park Service’s 2017 foundation document lists climate change and coral bleaching from rising sea temperatures among the threats to the park’s reefs, and warns that frequent storms and typhoons, long-term climate change and potential sea level rise threaten park facilities and World War II structures that were hastily built and not meant to last 60 years or more. [n] [n] [n]

facts.claim: 'For the people of Guam, war came early and stayed late'
Japan bombed Guam hours after Pearl Harbor (Dec. 7; Dec. 8 west of the date line); Japanese forces invaded Dec. 10, 1941

Feb.–Mar. 1942 island renamed Omiyajima; keibitai (Japanese naval police) govern; 1943 English forbidden; Chamorros suspected of hiding family members wanted by the Japanese or aiding Americans harassed, beaten, tortured or executed

1944: Chamorro men, women and children labor at bayonet point in fields, build defenses, dig hundreds of shelter caves; early July 10,000–15,000 Chamorros forced to march to jungle camps with little food or water; many do not survive
July 21, 1944: 55,000 U.S. troops land on Asan and Agat beaches; Aug. 10 Guam declared secure; over 7,000 American and about 17,500 Japanese casualties
Park established August 18, 1978
Seven units within, adjacent to and surrounding the villages of Asan, Piti and Agat; invasion beaches, pillboxes, caves preserved
Piti Guns: three Japanese 140mm coastal defense guns hauled in by Chamorros under forced labor in 1944
Agat Unit: WWII latrine foundation, remnant of former refugee camps where thousands of Chamorros were left homeless
Asan Bay Overlook memorial wall lists American servicemen who died defending Guam in 1941 and liberating it in 1944, and the people of Guam who suffered and died during the 31 months of occupation
More than half the park's area is coral reef; most biologically diverse park in the national park system
First settlers, referred to as Chamorro, believed to have arrived from Southeast Asia only residents in Oceania who cultivated rice
The more affluent lived in houses atop 12-foot stone pillars called latte stones; the less affluent used wooden posts
1671 (September) organized assault on a fortified church by 2,000 Chamorro, siege ~40 days; disease and fighting left approximately 3,700 residents by 1710
After 1898 the U.S. immediately transformed over a third of the island into a military installation; Navy officer immediately appointed governor; pattern of military control for almost seventy years
Figure 7-1 (Guam Director of Land Management, 1952): military 49,128 (1950) to 58,744 (1952); private 64,454 to 46,813
October 15, 1977 statute empowered District Court of Guam to hear claims for land obtained 1944–1963 by means other than fair judicial condemnation
Seventy-plus-year pattern of military control engendered deep local resentment and mistrust — the political and social environment in which the park was born

Widespread bleaching on Guam's shallow reefs every year 2013–2017; 2014–2015 El Niño heat stress and extreme low tides ravaged branching Acropora on reef flats including a site in WAPA's Asan unit; 2017 worst year on record for heat stress and bleaching
